Example 1: Market fear and the news, over time
The variables. The CBOE Volatility Index (VIX) is the options market’s 30-day forward-looking measure of expected S&P 500 volatility — Wall Street’s “fear gauge.” The San Francisco Fed Daily News Sentiment Index is a daily sentiment score built by scoring economics-related articles across 16 major U.S. newspapers, smoothed into a continuous time series back to 1980. Both are daily, both are United States–based, and both are free to download.
Sourcing. VIX: CBOE Volatility Index, retrieved from FRED (Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis), series VIXCLS. News sentiment: Shapiro, Sudhof & Wilson (2020), Daily News Sentiment Index, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco. The overlap between the two series runs from January 3, 2000 to September 11, 2026 — 6,747 trading days.

The levels of VIX and news sentiment are strongly negatively correlated (r = −0.61): when the market is fearful, the news is gloomier, and vice versa. That is the correlation most people mean when they say “the market and the news move together.” But when the same two series are converted to day-over-day changes — did VIX and sentiment move together from one day to the next — the correlation collapses to essentially zero. That gap is itself the lesson: a strong correlation in levels can come almost entirely from both series drifting through the same multi-year regimes (calm 2000s, the 2008 crisis, COVID, etc.), not from any tight day-to-day linkage between newsroom tone and options pricing.

title: Fear Gauges and Headlines
section: Why the correlation might not mean what it looks like
text:
Why the correlation might not mean what it looks like
In the time-series example, the headline result (r = −0.61 in levels, r ≈ 0 in changes) points to a specific third factor: the macroeconomic regime. VIX and news sentiment both drift with the business cycle — both were low and calm for most of the mid-2000s, both moved sharply in 2008 and again in 2020 — so a big share of their correlation in levels is really both series independently tracking the same underlying economic conditions, rather than one driving the other day to day. The fact that the correlation nearly disappears in first differences is the tell.
In the cross-country example, the plausible third factor is different: EPU counts newspaper mentions of policy uncertainty, while an implied-volatility index prices option-market risk. A country can generate a great deal of uncertainty-flavored news coverage — coalition politics, fiscal debates, regulatory fights — without that translating into elevated pricing of equity risk, and Germany in July 2026 looks like exactly that case. The two variables are related in principle (both are trying to measure “uncertainty”) but are constructed from different underlying processes (text mentions vs. option prices), which is enough to decouple them country by country.

title: Wages vs. Prices: A Century of American Pay
text: Data Story  ·  United States  ·  Wages and Prices

title: Wages vs. Prices: A Century of American Pay
text:
Picking the right yardsticks
Before plotting anything, two questions needed answers: whose wages, and whose prices?
For wages, the cleanest candidate would be something like median household income — except the Census Bureau didn’t start publishing that until 1947. Nominal GDP per capita reaches back further, but it blends labor income with capital income and divides by total population rather than hours worked, so it answers “how rich is the country,” not “how far does an hour of work go.” The series economic historians actually use for this comparison is average hourly earnings of production workers in manufacturing. The Bureau of Labor Statistics has published it continuously since 1939; the NBER’s Macrohistory Database and the economic-history site MeasuringWorth extend it back to 1900 by linking two earlier academic series. It’s the standard choice for a century-long view, for the simple reason that nothing else covers the period as consistently.
That choice comes with a real caveat. It’s a manufacturing, blue-collar measure in an economy that has moved overwhelmingly into services, and it counts cash wages only — leaving out the employer-paid health insurance and retirement contributions that have grown from negligible to a large share of total compensation since the 1960s. Total compensation almost certainly grew faster than the cash-wage line below, especially in recent decades; this chart is deliberately the more conservative, more consistently measured slice of the story.
For prices, the Consumer Price Index is the more straightforward call: it’s the standard cost-of-living yardstick, built to track what a household actually spends on housing, food, transportation, and the like. The Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis publishes a continuous CPI series back to 1800, splicing the official BLS index (1913–present) onto three earlier historical estimates the BLS itself compiled for its Handbook of Labor Statistics.








Index, 1900 = 100, log scale (a straight line on this scale means a constant growth rate, which makes it possible to compare series growing at very different speeds on one axis). Dotted lines mark 1929 (onset of the Depression) and 1973, the year economists most often cite as the start of the long real-wage slowdown. Click any legend item to isolate that line. Wage series splices five underlying sources; Consumer Price Index splices four. See methodology and sources below.



Nominal wage growth, 1900–2025 194× 15.2¢/hr in 1900 → $29.51/hr in 2025, average factory pay


Price level growth, 1900–2025 38.7× What $1.00 bought in 1900 costs $38.70 today

Real wages, 1973 → 2025 −0.5% Essentially flat for half a century, despite nominal pay rising 7× further

title: Wages vs. Prices: A Century of American Pay
text:
Three eras of pay
The 126-year run breaks into three distinct phases, and the breakpoints aren’t subtle.
1900–1929. Factory wages roughly quadrupled in nominal terms, but World War I inflation took a large bite out of the gain. Real purchasing power still rose by close to 80% over these three decades — a genuine, if uneven, improvement.
The Depression and the war, 1930–1945. Nominal wages fell sharply in the early 1930s, but prices fell even faster, so real wages held up better than the headlines from the period suggest, before climbing again under wartime labor demand and the wage and price controls of the early 1940s.
The postwar golden age, 1946–1973. This is where the real wage line is steepest. Driven by strong productivity growth, high union density in manufacturing, and a tight postwar labor market, real factory pay nearly tripled again between the end of the war and 1973 — the single best sustained stretch in the dataset.
Since 1973. The real wage index has barely moved: 504 in 1973, 502 in 2025. Nominal wages and consumer prices have both continued climbing — nominal pay is up more than sevenfold since 1973 alone — but almost none of that nominal gain has translated into added purchasing power for this particular measure of pay. Economists point to several plausible, overlapping explanations for the slowdown: the shrinking share of the workforce employed in manufacturing itself, declining private-sector union membership, the erosion of the real value of the minimum wage, a shift in total compensation toward non-wage benefits that this wage-only measure doesn’t capture, and the effects of automation and global trade competition on demand for manufacturing labor specifically. There’s no single, settled answer in the research, and the relative weight of each factor remains actively debated.

title: Wages vs. Prices: A Century of American Pay
section: What this measure can’t tell you
text:
What this measure can’t tell you
A national average hides as much as it reveals. It says nothing about how pay has diverged by region, industry, education, race, or gender over the same period, and it says nothing about the well-documented widening gap between average and median pay since the 1980s — a separate and important part of the inequality story that a single average wage line cannot show. It is also, deliberately, a manufacturing-sector measure in an economy where manufacturing’s employment share has fallen for decades; a similar exercise using service-sector or all-private-sector pay (available only from 1964 onward) would likely tell a somewhat different recent story. And because it tracks cash wages only, it understates how total compensation — wages plus benefits — has grown, particularly since employer-sponsored health insurance became widespread. Future posts on this site could push further into any of these threads: a sectoral breakdown, a look at the minimum wage specifically, or a comparison against productivity growth.


Sources: Wages — U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Average Hourly Earnings of Production and Nonsupervisory Employees, Manufacturing (series CES3000000008), 1939–2025; National Bureau of Economic Research Macrohistory Database, series a08050a (Paul H. Douglas, Real Wages in the United States, 1890–1926) for 1900–1919 and series a08050b (National Industrial Conference Board, Wages, Hours, and Employment in the United States: 1914–1936) for 1920–1933; 1934–1938 linearly interpolated between these two series due to a gap in consistent annual reporting during the NIRA/early-FLSA transition. Prices — Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis, Consumer Price Index, 1800– (splicing BLS historical cost-of-living estimates for 1900–1912 with the official Consumer Price Index, 1913–2025).

title: Cameras After the Smartphone

title: Cameras After the Smartphone
text:
Finding a real time series
CIPA, the Japanese trade association whose members include Canon, Nikon, Sony, Fujifilm, Panasonic, and Olympus/OM Digital, has published monthly worldwide shipment data since the 1990s and is the industry-standard source everyone from Statista to DPReview ultimately cites. The association’s own historical PDF archive isn’t set up for scraping, so the series below is reconstructed from CIPA’s published monthly and annual releases as reported by CIPA itself and cross-checked against PetaPixel, DPReview, Nikon Rumors, and Statista, rather than pulled from a single downloadable file.
2007 is where a clean, comparable annual series becomes possible: that’s the first year CIPA’s own releases split shipments into “built-in lens” (compact) and “interchangeable lens” (DSLR-and-later-mirrorless) totals, and it’s also the year worldwide shipments first broke 100 million units. Before 2007, comparable digital-era data exists (roughly 5 million units shipped in 1995, the digital camera’s standing start) but isn’t broken out by camera type, so it’s mentioned qualitatively rather than charted.
Splitting that “interchangeable lens” total into DSLR and mirrorless separately is a harder problem, because CIPA didn’t report the two as distinct categories in its own headline releases until well into the format’s life. Mirrorless launched in September 2008 (Panasonic’s Lumix G1) and was a rounding error for years afterward, so 2007–2011 below shows essentially all interchangeable-lens shipments as DSLR. From 2012 the mirrorless share is interpolated against known product milestones — Sony’s a7 brought full-frame mirrorless in 2013; Nikon and Canon didn’t commit to full-frame mirrorless systems of their own until 2018 — anchored to three points CIPA itself has published: mirrorless overtook DSLR within the interchangeable-lens category for the first time in 2020 (51.5%), reached 68.7% by 2022, and 80.5% by 2023. 2024 and 2025 are CIPA’s own reported figures. The interpolated stretch (2012–2019, and 2021) is flagged in the chart note below; treat it as the shape of the transition rather than exact annual counts.

title: Cameras After the Smartphone
section: The format war: who won the shrinking pie
text:
The format war: who won the shrinking pie
The total collapsed, but the mix inside it changed even more dramatically. In 2010, compact point-and-shoots — the cameras smartphones killed first — still accounted for 109 million of the 121.5 million units shipped, with DSLRs and the still-new mirrorless format (Panasonic’s Lumix G1, the first mirrorless model, had shipped roughly two years earlier) making up the remaining 12.5 million between them. By 2025, the compact category had shrunk to 2.4 million units but mirrorless had grown into the dominant force in the industry at 6.3 million units, while DSLRs — which Canon and Nikon have largely stopped developing — had fallen to just 691,000, kept alive mainly by Pentax and a market for cheap used bodies.

title: Cameras After the Smartphone
text:
Two different recoveries, one chart
The 2024–2025 uptick isn’t one story but two. At the top of the market, mirrorless bodies keep getting more expensive and more capable, and buyers — increasingly professionals and serious enthusiasts rather than casual shooters — keep paying for them; shipment value has grown faster than unit volume for several years running. At the bottom, a cohort too young to have owned a point-and-shoot the first time around has been driving demand for compact cameras like the Fujifilm X100 series and screen-free novelties like the Camp Snap, treating a dedicated camera as a deliberate alternative to a phone rather than a worse version of one. Both trends show up as growth in the same chart, but they’re selling to different customers for different reasons — which is presumably why CIPA’s own 2026 shipment forecasts still describe a wide range (6.3–7.4 million interchangeable-lens bodies) rather than a confident single number.

The 2010 compact/interchangeable-lens split is drawn from CIPA’s own reported totals for that year.

Two industries, one dataset problem
The camera side of this story is CIPA’s — the same worldwide shipment data used in our earlier post on the DSLR-to-mirrorless transition. The smartphone side comes from IDC’s Worldwide Quarterly Mobile Phone Tracker, the industry-standard source that most outlets (and Statista’s own smartphone-shipment statistics) ultimately cite. The two trackers don’t share a methodology — IDC counts all Android and iOS manufacturers combined, CIPA counts a defined list of Japanese-headquartered camera brands — but both report worldwide unit shipments to the same rough standard, which is what makes overlaying them meaningful.
2007–2009 smartphone totals are reconstructed estimates (IDC’s own press archive gets sparse before its 2010–2011 releases), interpolated between known points: Apple’s own reported 3.3 million iPhones in 2007, RIM’s roughly 20% share of a 175-million-unit market in 2009, and Nokia’s continued Symbian dominance through the period. 2010 onward are IDC’s own published totals, cited repeatedly across its press releases. Compact camera figures are CIPA’s, identical to the previous post.

title: The Camera in Everyone’s Pocket
section: The pioneer that got left behind
text:
The pioneer that got left behind
BlackBerry’s own trajectory is a case study within the case study. RIM held its cameras back for years on principle — the BlackBerry 7230 (2003) had Bluetooth and a color screen but no camera; corporate IT departments and government buildings were actively hostile to camera phones at the time, and RIM’s whole business was selling into those buildings. The Pearl broke with that policy in 2006, and it worked: RIM’s shipments roughly tripled over the next four years, peaking around 2011. Then BlackBerry OS’s browser, app ecosystem, and touchscreen kept losing to iOS and Android, the camera-first feature that once differentiated the Pearl became table stakes on every phone, and BlackBerry’s hardware shipments collapsed even faster than they’d grown.

Shipments fell below 1 million annually by 2016, after which BlackBerry-branded phones were made under license by TCL rather than by BlackBerry itself.

title: The Camera in Everyone’s Pocket
section: The feature that won wasn’t the camera
text:
The feature that won wasn’t the camera
It’s tempting to read this as “camera phones killed cameras,” and directionally that’s right — but BlackBerry’s own arc shows the camera alone was never the differentiator. RIM added a perfectly serviceable camera in 2006 and gained share for years afterward; it lost that share to companies that paired a camera with instant sharing, an app ecosystem, and a touchscreen built around photos and video rather than email. The compact camera didn’t lose to “a camera in a phone” — it lost to a phone where the camera was one part of a always-with-you, always-connected package that no dedicated camera, however good the sensor, could match. Which is also, per the previous post, exactly the gap mirrorless cameras and revived point-and-shoots are now trying to compete on different terms altogether: image quality and a deliberate, single-purpose object, rather than convenience.

title: How Much Has Boston Warmed? 133 Years of Daily Highs and Lows
text:
One city, two weather stations
A 133-year daily temperature record for any single American city doesn’t come from one continuous source. Boston’s does not either. From 1893 to 1935, the official readings came from a downtown “Boston City” station; since 1936, they’ve come from Boston Logan International Airport, built on filled tidal flats in East Boston. Both feed into the same NOAA-maintained record used here, and splicing stations like this is standard practice in long climate series — it’s the same approach the National Weather Service itself uses to construct Boston’s official climate normals.
It’s also a genuine caveat rather than a footnote. Airport stations tend to sit on open, paved ground surrounded by jet exhaust and less vegetation than a downtown site, which can nudge readings — especially daytime highs — slightly warmer than an old-city location would show for identical weather. The 1936 station change is marked on the chart below; it’s worth keeping in mind when comparing eras on either side of that line.








Annual average of daily high and low temperatures, Boston, MA, 1893–2025. Dotted line marks 1936, when the official record switches from the downtown Boston City station to Boston Logan International Airport. Green line is a trailing 10-year average of the annual mean temperature ((high + low) / 2), smoothing year-to-year noise to show the underlying trend. Click any legend item to isolate that line.



Warmest year on record 2021 Average high 61.8°F, average low 47.3°F


Coldest year on record 1904 Average high 55.1°F, average low 39.3°F


Daytime high, 1893–1902 → 2016–2025 +3.1°F Decade average rose from 57.7°F to 60.9°F


Nighttime low, 1893–1902 → 2016–2025 +4.0°F Decade average rose from 42.1°F to 46.1°F — nights are warming faster than days

title: How Much Has Boston Warmed? 133 Years of Daily Highs and Lows
section: Nights are warming faster than days
text:
Nights are warming faster than days
The gap between the two lines has narrowed over time, and that’s the more interesting half of the story. If Boston were simply getting a uniformly warmer version of the same climate, the high and low lines would have shifted upward by roughly the same amount. Instead, the average low has risen about four degrees since the 1890s, versus roughly three degrees for the average high.
This isn’t unique to Boston — nighttime lows warming faster than daytime highs is a well-documented pattern across much of the United States, and several forces plausibly contribute: cloud cover and humidity trap outgoing heat overnight, urban and airport development reduces how quickly the ground radiates heat away after sunset, and warming winters mean fewer of the historically frigid, clear, dry nights that used to pull the coldest lows down hard. Because Logan Airport itself has been built up substantially since 1936 — more pavement, more infrastructure, more heat-retaining surface around the immediate station — some of this narrowing could also reflect the station’s own changing surroundings rather than the regional climate alone. Both are almost certainly part of the picture; disentangling exactly how much is beyond what this single-station record can settle.

title: How Much Has Boston Warmed? 133 Years of Daily Highs and Lows
section: A record increasingly stacked with recent years
text:
A record increasingly stacked with recent years
The chart’s ranking tells its own story. Of the ten warmest years since 1893, eight occurred in 2010 or later: 2021, 2012, 2023, 2010, 2024, 2022, 2020, and 2016. But the list isn’t a clean, monotonic march upward — 1949 and 1953 also crack the top ten, both comfortably warmer than most years around them. Those two mid-century years are a reminder that a single unusually warm year has always been possible in Boston’s climate; what’s changed is the odds. A “top-ten warmest year” used to be a rare, scattered event across the twentieth century. Now it is the typical outcome of any given year in the 2010s and 2020s.

title: How Much Has Boston Warmed? 133 Years of Daily Highs and Lows
section: What a single station can’t tell you
text:
What a single station can’t tell you
This is one station’s daily-average record, and it leaves real gaps. It says nothing about precipitation, snowfall, or storm intensity — a separate and increasingly important part of New England’s changing climate. It says nothing about single-day extremes: a year with a mild average can still contain a record-breaking heat wave or cold snap that this chart smooths away entirely. It reflects one site’s specific microclimate — coastal, low-lying, airport-adjacent — which won’t match temperature trends recorded a few miles inland or at higher elevation. And because the underlying source splices two station records at 1936, some caution is warranted when comparing eras directly across that seam. A natural next post on this thread would push into extremes directly: the frequency of 90°F+ days, or how the length of Boston’s frost-free growing season has changed over the same 133 years.


Sources: Annual average daily high and low temperatures for Boston, Massachusetts, 1893–2025, based on NOAA climate data (Boston City station, 1893–1935; Boston Logan International Airport, GHCND:USW00014739, 1936–2025), as compiled by Extreme Weather Watch.

title: Life Expectancy and National Income: Cross-Sectional and Within-Country Correlations
text: Machine Learning for Social Science  ·  Boston, MA

title: Life Expectancy and National Income: Cross-Sectional and Within-Country Correlations
text:
Abstract
Design. Observational correlational study with three components: a cross-section of countries, a single-country time series, and within-country time series for every country with sufficient data. Objective. To estimate and compare the correlation between life expectancy and GDP per capita across countries and within countries over time. Methods. Publicly available national statistics; Pearson correlation coefficients on untransformed and log-transformed income, and on year-over-year changes. Results. Across 175 countries in 2023–2024, r = 0.86 (log income; p = 8.6×10−53). Within the United States, 1960–2024, r = 0.97 (log income; p = 2.5×10−40). Across 203 countries, the median within-country correlation was 0.87, but 19 countries had significant negative correlations, several of them low-income countries where life expectancy rose by more than 20 years while GDP per capita fell. Correlations of year-over-year changes were close to zero in most countries (median r = 0.10). Conclusion. The strong level correlations largely reflect shared long-run trends. Large health gains occurred in some countries without income growth, which is consistent with, but does not establish, a role for health improvements that do not depend on GDP growth.

title: Life Expectancy and National Income: Cross-Sectional and Within-Country Correlations
text:
Introduction

Background and rationale
The association between national income and population health is one of the best-documented regularities in economic demography. Preston (1975) showed that across countries, life expectancy rises steeply with income at low incomes and flattens at high incomes. That finding, the Preston curve, is cross-sectional: different countries compared at one point in time.
Whether the same association holds within a country as it develops over time is a separate question. A relationship that is strong across units need not describe the path of any single unit, a problem known as the ecological fallacy (Robinson, 1950). Preston himself found that the cross-sectional curve shifted upward over the twentieth century, so that most of the gain in life expectancy over that period could not be attributed to income growth along a fixed curve.
Correlation is the simplest tool for asking whether two variables move together, and it can be applied in both dimensions: across units at a point in time, and within a unit across time. This study applies the same statistic in both dimensions to the same pair of variables, so that differences in the results can be attributed to the design rather than to the method.


Objectives

To estimate the correlation between life expectancy and GDP per capita across countries at one point in time (cross-sectional design).
To estimate the same correlation within the United States over 65 years (single-country time-series design).
To estimate the within-country time-series correlation for every country with sufficient data, and to describe how it varies across countries and regions.
To consider what a correlation coefficient can and cannot establish in each design.

title: Life Expectancy and National Income: Cross-Sectional and Within-Country Correlations
text:
Methods

Study design
Three designs are reported. (i) Cross-section: each country contributes one observation at approximately the same point in time. (ii) Single-country time series: the United States contributes one observation per year from 1960 to 2024. (iii) Multi-country time series: for each country, a separate correlation is computed across that country’s own years, producing one correlation coefficient per country. All designs are purely observational.


Setting
The cross-section uses the most recent year available in each source (GDP per capita: 2023; life expectancy: most recent CIA World Factbook estimate, referenced 2024). Both time-series designs cover 1960 to 2024, the full span of the World Development Indicators (WDI) series.


Participants (units of analysis)
Cross-section: all countries and territories with both a life expectancy and a GDP per capita value in the sources below, matched by name with manual reconciliation of naming differences. Of 229 countries and territories with a life expectancy estimate, 175 (76%) had a matching GDP figure and were included.
United States time series: all 65 years from 1960 to 2024; none missing.
Multi-country time series: all World Bank economies in the WDI files, excluding regional and income-group aggregates, with at least 20 years in which both series were reported. 203 economies met this criterion. The median number of years per country was 65 (range 20–65). Countries were grouped by the World Bank region listed in the WDI country metadata, used as published (which places Afghanistan, Pakistan and Malta in Middle East & North Africa, and Greenland in Europe & Central Asia).


Variables
Outcome: life expectancy at birth, in years: the average number of years a newborn would live if the age-specific mortality rates of that year persisted throughout its life.
Exposure: GDP per capita. In the cross-section, current US dollars. In both time-series designs, constant 2015 US dollars, which removes inflation so that changes over time reflect real income.

Bias
Four sources of bias are noted. First, the cross-section combines life expectancy and GDP from different producers and reference years. Second, WDI life expectancy for many low- and middle-income countries is modeled by the UN Population Division rather than measured annually from vital registration; modeled series are smooth, which mechanically weakens correlations of year-over-year changes. Third, no adjustment was made for variables that affect both income and health (education, disease environment, conflict, governance). Fourth, in the time-series designs, calendar time itself is a common driver: medical and public health technology improved throughout the period regardless of any one country’s income.


Study size
Study size was determined by data availability: 175 countries in the cross-section, 65 years for the United States, and 203 countries (median 65 years each) in the multi-country time series. No power calculation was performed.


Quantitative variables
GDP per capita was analyzed untransformed and natural-log transformed. The log transform was included because the relationship is known to be concave, and a Pearson correlation on untransformed income understates a strong but curved association. Life expectancy was analyzed in years.


Statistical methods
All associations are Pearson product-moment correlation coefficients. The formula is the same in every design; only the index changes.
Cross-section, across countries i = 1, …, n:
\[
r_{\text{CS}} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar{x})(y_i-\bar{y})}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar{x})^2\;\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i-\bar{y})^2}}
\]
Time series for country c, across years t = 1, …, Tc:
\[
r_{c} = \frac{\sum_{t=1}^{T_c}(x_{ct}-\bar{x}_c)(y_{ct}-\bar{y}_c)}{\sqrt{\sum_{t=1}^{T_c}(x_{ct}-\bar{x}_c)^2\;\sum_{t=1}^{T_c}(y_{ct}-\bar{y}_c)^2}}
\]
where x is GDP per capita (or its natural log) and y is life expectancy.
Significance. Each coefficient is tested against the null hypothesis of no correlation using
\[
t = r\sqrt{\frac{n-2}{1-r^2}}, \qquad p = 2\,\Pr\left(T_{n-2} > |t|\right),
\]
with n the number of countries (cross-section) or years (time series). Because t grows with both r and n, strong correlations in long series produce extremely small p-values. The test assumes independent observations.
Year-over-year changes. To separate co-movement from shared trends, the within-country correlation was also computed on annual changes, using consecutive years only:
\[
\Delta y_{ct} = y_{ct} - y_{c,t-1}, \qquad \Delta x_{ct} = \ln X_{ct} - \ln X_{c,t-1},
\]
where Δx is approximately the annual growth rate of GDP per capita. If life expectancy and income are linked year to year, Δx and Δy should be correlated. If they merely trend together over decades, the level correlation will be high while the change correlation is near zero.
No regression model was fit. This choice is deliberate and is returned to in the Conclusion.
When a correlation is a valid tool, and when it is not. A Pearson correlation validly summarizes the strength and direction of a linear (or, after transformation, monotonic) association, and its significance test is valid when observations are independent. It becomes an unreliable guide to the underlying relationship in three situations relevant here. First, when a third variable moves both x and y (confounding). Second, when the data are aggregates: a correlation across country averages can differ in sign or size from the correlation within any country, and vice versa (the ecological fallacy). Third, in time series, when both variables share a common trend: two unrelated series that both rise for decades will correlate strongly, with time as the omitted third variable (Yule, 1926; Granger and Newbold, 1974). In that case consecutive observations are also strongly autocorrelated, so the effective sample size is far smaller than the number of years and the p-values above are too small.
Why life expectancy and GDP per capita are a good test case. The relationship is real, large and well replicated, with plausible mechanisms (income buys nutrition, sanitation and medical care), so it is not a trivial example. It also displays all three pitfalls: income is correlated with many confounders across countries; the cross-sectional curve is known to have shifted over time; and life expectancy rose almost everywhere after 1960 through medical and public health advances that were partly independent of national income.

title: Life Expectancy and National Income: Cross-Sectional and Within-Country Correlations
text:
Discussion

Key results
The cross-section and the US time series both show a strong positive correlation in levels. Extending the time-series design to 203 countries shows that the US result is common but not universal: about one in four countries has a level correlation below 0.5, and 19 have significant negative correlations. In nearly all countries, the correlation of year-over-year changes is close to zero.


Can health improve without income growth?
The countries in Table 3 are the most direct evidence in this study on that question. Liberia, Niger, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Haiti and Madagascar each gained more than 20 years of life expectancy over a period in which their real GDP per capita fell. Whatever drove those gains, it was not domestic income growth. This is consistent with a long literature arguing that mortality can fall substantially at low income: Caldwell (1986) on “routes to low mortality in poor countries,” Riley (2008) on low-income countries with high longevity, and Cutler, Deaton and Lleras-Muney (2006), who argue that the spread of knowledge and technology, such as vaccination, oral rehydration, antibiotics and malaria control, explains more of the mortality decline than income does. Much of this was delivered through public programs and international health financing rather than private spending, which points toward a policy case that health investment need not wait for growth.
Four cautions apply before drawing that conclusion from these data:

The counterfactual is unknown. A correlation cannot say whether these countries would have gained even more with income growth. Gains without growth are not evidence that growth does not matter.
The drivers are not measured here. No policy variable was observed. The pattern is consistent with health policy, imported medical technology, external aid and falling fertility, but this study does not distinguish among them.
Not all negative correlations reflect health policy. In the oil economies and small island territories, GDP per capita fell from already high levels while life expectancy continued to rise. These cases reflect commodity prices and population growth rather than health gains achieved in poverty.
Measurement. Life expectancy in many low-income countries is modeled rather than measured each year, which makes the series smoother than the underlying reality.

The appropriate conclusion is that the data are consistent with large health gains without income growth, and that this hypothesis merits a design that can test it: for example, relating within-country changes in life expectancy to measured health interventions such as vaccination coverage or public health spending.


Limitations
This is a correlational analysis of unadjusted, aggregated national statistics. No confounders were controlled for. In both time-series designs the level correlations are dominated by shared trends, and because consecutive years are strongly autocorrelated, the reported level p-values overstate statistical significance; the effective number of independent observations is far smaller than the number of years. The cross-section combines two data producers and two reference years. Finally, a single Pearson r reports the strength of an association but not its slope, so it cannot show whether the cross-sectional and within-country relationships have the same shape.


Interpretation
Life expectancy and income are strongly correlated across countries and, in levels, within most countries over time. The within-country level correlation mainly reflects the fact that life expectancy rose almost everywhere after 1960: where income also rose, the correlation is strongly positive; where income fell, it is strongly negative; and year-to-year changes are only weakly related in either case. A correlation coefficient cannot distinguish a direct effect of income from a common trend, and the multi-country results suggest the common trend accounts for much of what the single-country US correlation appears to show.


Generalizability
The cross-sectional estimate describes the 175 included countries at one point in time and should not be read as describing the path of any single country. The US time series describes the United States only. The multi-country results show directly that within-country relationships vary widely, and that the United States is an example of the most common pattern rather than a representative case.

title: Life Expectancy and National Income: Cross-Sectional and Within-Country Correlations
text:
Conclusion and next steps
All three designs return strong correlations in levels, but the multi-country analysis shows that the within-country correlation can be strong and positive, near zero, or strong and negative, and that it largely disappears in year-over-year changes. The next post in this series will fit unadjusted ordinary least squares (OLS) regressions to the same data. That adds what a correlation cannot provide: an explicit slope (years of life expectancy per unit of log income) that can be compared directly between the cross-section and the within-country series; an R² for each design; and residual plots showing where countries depart from the fitted relationship. Regression will remain unadjusted for confounders, and the trend problem identified here will carry over to it, which motivates later steps such as models in differences and models with country and year effects.

The one that doesn’t fit on the chart: camcorders
The Flip Video camera is worth a stat card of its own because its rise-and-fall happened almost entirely within the smartphone-camera era, compressed into five years rather than a decade. Pure Digital Technologies launched the Flip in 2006 as a stripped-down, pocket-sized camcorder that did one thing well: record decent video and get it onto a computer with a flip-out USB connector, no cables required. It sold nearly 5 million units by September 2010 and briefly became the #1-selling camcorder brand in the US. Cisco, which had bought the brand for $590 million in 2009, killed it in April 2011 — one day before a new model was due on shelves. The reasoning was almost apologetic: smartphone video had gotten good enough, and more importantly, uploadable enough, that a device whose entire pitch was “simple to shoot, simple to share” had nothing left to be simple about.

The feature that made all of this permanent: sharing
Every product on that chart lost a hardware race, but the deeper thing they lost was a distribution race. A camera, a GPS unit, or an MP3 player was a closed loop — whatever it captured or calculated stayed on the device until you plugged it into a computer. What made the smartphone different wasn’t just that it combined those features; it’s that whatever it captured could be online, in front of other people, in seconds. That only mattered because, starting almost exactly when the iPhone did, hundreds of millions of people suddenly had somewhere to put it.

Back to BlackBerry, one more time
This is the piece that makes the BlackBerry story make sense as more than a punchline. BlackBerry added a camera in 2006, a full two years before Instagram existed and before Facebook had cracked 100 million users — the camera was, for a while, ahead of anywhere good to put the photos. By the time Instagram launched in October 2010, BlackBerry’s own App World was over a year old, chronically thin on quality apps, and its browser couldn’t render most of the mobile web properly. RIM had the hardware pattern right in 2006 and the distribution pattern wrong for the rest of the decade — which, across every device on the chart above, turns out to be the difference that mattered.

A deliberately partial picture
This post is narrower in scope than the temperature posts on this site, and it’s worth saying why up front. Boston’s annual average high and low temperatures are compiled year-by-year in public, ready-to-use datasets going back to the 1890s. Wind is not treated the same way: the underlying daily and annual wind measurements exist in NOAA’s archives, but nobody has published the full year-by-year average wind speed series in a form that’s readily accessible without a direct bulk download from NOAA’s climate data systems.
What follows, then, is built entirely from specific, documented reference points — individual facts reported by NOAA/NCEI, the Iowa Environmental Mesonet, and the Boston Globe’s weather coverage — rather than a reconstructed year-by-year time series. Where a number below is a single documented data point rather than part of a continuous series, that’s noted explicitly. A fuller post, with an actual annual series, is a natural thing to come back to if a direct route to NOAA’s underlying station data opens up.

title: Boston’s Windiest Year: What the Record Actually Shows
section: Gusts up, sustained wind more ambiguous
text:
Gusts up, sustained wind more ambiguous
Gusts and sustained wind speed are genuinely different measurements, not just two ways of describing the same thing. Sustained wind speed is the average flow over a two-minute stretch; a gust is a brief, sharp spike that can last a few seconds to half a minute. Boston’s 2025 story is really a story about gusts specifically: through the first half of 2025, gusts were averaging nearly 32.6 mph, more than 2 mph above the previous record pace set in 2010, and Logan recorded gusts of 30 mph or higher on 165 days that year — roughly two and a half times the yearly average for days that gusty.
Sustained wind speed tells a more ambiguous story. Through the first half of 2025, sustained wind speed averaged 12.28 mph — the highest since 2000, and above the trailing 30-year average — but still below the full 89-year average for the station. Taken at face value, that means Logan’s sustained winds have historically run higher, on average, over the full 20th-century record than they have in the more recent 30-year normal period, even as 2025’s gusts were setting all-time records. That’s a genuinely interesting tension worth investigating further, but it isn’t one this post can fully resolve without the complete annual series in hand.

title: Boston’s Windiest Year: What the Record Actually Shows
section: Why Boston is windy at all
text:
Why Boston is windy at all
Boston’s wind isn’t a fluke of any one year. Among major U.S. cities, Boston is the single windiest, with average wind speeds about 2 mph higher than second-place Chicago (the city that actually carries the “Windy City” nickname) and roughly twice the average wind speed of Phoenix, the calmest major U.S. city. The explanation researchers point to is location: Logan sits on the coast, close to the North Atlantic’s active storm track, which is also why a warming ocean and atmosphere can plausibly push the upper end of storm intensity higher without necessarily changing the day-to-day average by much — a distinction that may help explain why 2025 broke gust records so clearly while its sustained-wind story stayed more mixed.

title: Does Income Growth Raise Life Expectancy? Country-by-Country Regressions in Levels and Five-Year Differences
text:
Abstract
Design. Observational study using country-specific time-series regressions. Objective. To estimate, for each country, the association between GDP per capita and life expectancy in levels, and between five-year changes in GDP per capita and five-year changes in life expectancy. Setting and participants. 106 countries with World Bank data on both variables from 1960, observed annually from 1960 to 2024 (levels) and over twelve non-overlapping five-year intervals from 1960 to 2020 (differences). Methods. Unadjusted bivariate OLS. In the levels model, income is measured as log growth since 1960, so the constant is the fitted life expectancy at the country’s 1960 income. In the difference model, the constant is the expected five-year gain in life expectancy at zero income growth. Results. In levels, the median slope was 10.0 years per unit of log income (6.9 years per doubling), positive and significant in 92 of 106 countries, with a median R² of 0.81. In five-year differences, the median slope fell to 1.5 and was significant in only 12 countries; the median R² was 0.08. The constant was positive and significant in 72 countries. Pooling all 1,272 country-periods, life expectancy rose 1.34 years per five years at zero growth, and 10% faster income growth over five years was associated with an additional 0.17 years (p = 3.7×10−5; R² = 0.026). Conclusion. Income growth is associated with gains in life expectancy, but the association is small: about a tenth of the average five-year gain. Most of the gain is in the constant, which in this model is the improvement that occurs without income growth.

title: Does Income Growth Raise Life Expectancy? Country-by-Country Regressions in Levels and Five-Year Differences
text:
Introduction

Background and rationale
Across countries, life expectancy rises with income, steeply at low incomes and more slowly at high incomes (Preston, 1975). The previous post in this series showed that within most countries the two series are also strongly correlated over time, with a median within-country correlation of 0.87. It also showed that correlations of year-over-year changes are close to zero, and that a number of countries gained more than 20 years of life expectancy while their GDP per capita fell.
Correlation has two limits for the question that matters for policy. First, it measures the tightness of an association, not its size: a correlation of 0.97 could correspond to a large or a trivial effect of income. Second, in levels it cannot separate an association between income and health from the fact that both tend to rise over time. OLS regression addresses the first limit directly by estimating a slope. Fitting the regression in differences partly addresses the second, because differencing removes anything constant about a country, and the constant term in a difference regression captures the average improvement that occurs regardless of growth.


Objectives

For each country, to estimate the association between the level of GDP per capita and the level of life expectancy, with the constant anchored at the country’s 1960 income.
For each country, to estimate the association between five-year growth in GDP per capita and the five-year change in life expectancy.
To estimate the average five-year association across all countries (pooled), and how much of the average gain in life expectancy it accounts for.
To compare the levels and difference estimates and describe what each can and cannot show.

title: Does Income Growth Raise Life Expectancy? Country-by-Country Regressions in Levels and Five-Year Differences
text:
Methods

Study design
Observational, country-specific time-series regressions, with a pooled regression across countries for the difference model. Each country is analyzed separately, so countries are compared only with their own past.


Setting
Annual data, 1960 to 2024, from the World Bank World Development Indicators (WDI), last updated 13 July 2026. The difference model uses the five-yearly observations 1960, 1965, …, 2020, giving twelve non-overlapping five-year intervals per country.


Participants (units of analysis)
All World Bank economies, excluding regional and income-group aggregates, with both life expectancy and GDP per capita reported for 1960, which is required to anchor the constant. 106 economies met this criterion, and all 106 also had complete data for every five-year point from 1960 to 2020. For the levels model, 105 countries contributed all 65 years; Syria’s GDP series ends in 2022 (63 years). The requirement of 1960 data excludes most countries that became independent after 1960, including the former Soviet republics and much of Eastern Europe, as well as countries without early national accounts (see Bias).
Countries are grouped by the World Bank region listed in the WDI country metadata, used as published.


Variables
Outcome. Life expectancy at birth (LE), in years.
Exposure, levels model. Growth in GDP per capita since 1960, in log points:
\[
x_{ct} = \ln \text{GDP}_{ct} - \ln \text{GDP}_{c,1960},
\]
where GDP is GDP per capita in constant 2015 US dollars for country c in year t. By construction x = 0 in 1960, x = 0.69 when income has doubled, and x is negative when income is below its 1960 level.
Exposure, difference model. Five-year growth in GDP per capita, Δ5x, defined below.

Bias
Five sources of bias are noted. (1) Selection: requiring 1960 data restricts the sample to 106 countries and excludes most post-1960 states; the excluded countries may have different income and health trajectories. (2) Measurement: for many low- and middle-income countries, WDI life expectancy is modeled by the UN Population Division rather than measured annually, which smooths the series and weakens estimated associations with short-run income changes. (3) Confounding: the regressions are unadjusted; education, conflict, disease environment, governance and health spending may affect both income and life expectancy. (4) Common trends: in the levels model, calendar time is an omitted variable (addressed by the difference model). (5) Reverse causation: healthier populations may be more productive, so part of any association may run from health to income.


Study size
All eligible countries were included (106). The levels model uses up to 65 annual observations per country (6,888 country-years in total); the difference model uses 12 five-year changes per country (1,272 country-periods). No power calculation was performed. With 12 observations per country, the country-specific difference regressions have little power to detect small slopes.


Statistical methods
Levels model. For each country c, fit by OLS over its years t:
\[
LE_{ct} = \alpha_c + \beta_c\, x_{ct} + \varepsilon_{ct}.
\]
The OLS estimates are
\[
\hat{\beta}_c = \frac{\sum_t (x_{ct}-\bar{x}_c)(LE_{ct}-\overline{LE}_c)}{\sum_t (x_{ct}-\bar{x}_c)^2} = r_c\,\frac{s_{LE,c}}{s_{x,c}},
\qquad
\hat{\alpha}_c = \overline{LE}_c - \hat{\beta}_c\,\bar{x}_c ,
\]
where rc is the within-country correlation from the previous post and s denotes a standard deviation. The slope is the correlation rescaled into units: years of life expectancy per log point of income. In a regression with one explanatory variable, R² = r².
Why the constant is life expectancy at 1960 income. Because x = 0 when income equals its 1960 value, the fitted value at that income is
\[
\widehat{LE}_c\big|_{\,\text{GDP}=\text{GDP}_{c,1960}} = \hat{\alpha}_c + \hat{\beta}_c \cdot 0 = \hat{\alpha}_c .
\]
So α is the life expectancy the fitted line predicts at the country’s 1960 income. It is not the same as observed 1960 life expectancy, because the line need not pass through the 1960 point; the two are close when the line fits well.
Anchoring at 1960 changes only the constant, not the slope. If the same regression is written with uncentered log income, LE = a + b ln GDP, then b = β and
\[
a_c = \alpha_c - \beta_c \ln \text{GDP}_{c,1960},
\]
which is the predicted life expectancy at a GDP per capita of one dollar, a value with no meaning. For the United States, a = −10.3 years, while α = 69.3 years, close to the observed 1960 value of 69.8.
Interpreting the slope. A one-unit change in x is a change of one log point, an increase of about 172%. Two more useful scales are a doubling of income (β × ln 2 ≈ 0.69β) and a 10% increase (β × ln 1.1 ≈ 0.095β).
Five-year difference model. Define changes over non-overlapping five-year intervals, t = 1965, 1970, …, 2020:
\[
\Delta_5 LE_{ct} = LE_{ct} - LE_{c,t-5}, \qquad
\Delta_5 x_{ct} = x_{ct} - x_{c,t-5} = \ln \text{GDP}_{ct} - \ln \text{GDP}_{c,t-5}.
\]
Two things happen when the levels model is differenced. First, the 1960 anchor cancels: (ln GDPt − ln GDP1960) − (ln GDPt−5 − ln GDP1960) = ln GDPt − ln GDPt−5, so the choice of base year has no effect on this model. Second, the constant α cancels too. Suppose the levels relationship also contains a time trend λ, representing improvements in health that accrue each year regardless of income:
\[
LE_{ct} = \alpha_c + \beta_c\, x_{ct} + \lambda_c\, t + \varepsilon_{ct}.
\]
Differencing over five years gives
\[
\Delta_5 LE_{ct} = 5\lambda_c + \beta_c\,\Delta_5 x_{ct} + \Delta_5 \varepsilon_{ct}.
\]
This motivates the estimated difference model
\[
\Delta_5 LE_{ct} = \gamma_c + \delta_c\,\Delta_5 x_{ct} + u_{ct},
\]
where the slope δ estimates the association with income net of a linear trend, and the new constant γ (= 5λ) is the expected five-year change in life expectancy when income does not grow. In other words, the constant in the difference model measures the health improvement that occurs without income growth, the quantity the previous post could only describe.
Pooled difference model. To summarize across countries, the difference model was also fit to all 1,272 country-periods together, with a single γ and δ. Because the twelve observations from one country are not independent, standard errors were clustered by country:
\[
\widehat{V}(\hat{\theta}) = (X'X)^{-1}\Big(\sum_{g=1}^{G} X_g'\hat{u}_g\hat{u}_g'X_g\Big)(X'X)^{-1}\cdot\frac{G}{G-1}\cdot\frac{N-1}{N-k},
\]
with G = 106 countries, N country-periods and k = 2 parameters; p-values use a t distribution with G − 1 degrees of freedom.
Inference in the country-specific models. Country-specific standard errors are classical OLS standard errors. In the levels model they are too small, because consecutive annual observations are strongly autocorrelated (see the previous post); p-values for β should be read as descriptive. Non-overlapping five-year differences are much less affected.
Sensitivity analyses. The pooled difference model was re-estimated excluding the 2015–2020 interval, because 2020 life expectancy was lowered in many countries by the COVID-19 pandemic; separately for 1960–2000 and 2000–2020; and by World Bank income group (2024 classification).

Levels. The levels regressions look like strong evidence that income raises life expectancy. The median slope is 10.0 years per log point, equivalent to 6.9 years for each doubling of GDP per capita, positive and significant in 92 of 106 countries, with a median R² of 0.81. The constant behaves as the base-year algebra predicts: the median α is 56.7 years, and across countries α correlates 0.89 with observed 1960 life expectancy, typically within about 3 years. Where α departs from observed 1960 life expectancy, it flags an unusual base year. China is the clearest case: observed life expectancy in 1960 was 33.4 years, at the height of the famine of 1959–1961, while α is 56.6, the value its later trajectory implies for 1960 income.
Nine countries have significantly negative levels slopes, the same countries the previous post identified with negative correlations, including Madagascar, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Haiti, Niger and Liberia. A negative β does not mean income harms health; it means income fell while life expectancy rose.
Five-year differences. Once the trend is moved into the constant, the slope shrinks and becomes imprecise. The median δ is 1.53, about 15% of the median levels slope, and is significant in only 12 of 106 countries (11 positive, 1 negative). The median R² falls from 0.81 to 0.08. In contrast, the constant γ is positive in 105 of 106 countries (median 1.19 years per five years, interquartile range 0.89 to 1.78) and significantly positive in 72; none is significantly negative. For most countries, the regression attributes the bulk of the five-year gain in life expectancy to the constant rather than to income growth.

Across all country-periods, life expectancy rose by 1.34 years per five years when income did not grow (γ), and each additional log point of five-year income growth was associated with 1.74 more years (δ, p = 3.7×10−5). In practical terms, five years of income growth that is 10% faster is associated with 0.17 more years of life expectancy. The association is statistically clear but small: income growth explains 2.6% of the variation in five-year changes in life expectancy. At the sample’s average five-year growth of 0.084 log points, growth accounts for about 0.15 years (1.74 × 0.084) of the average five-year gain of 1.48 years, roughly one tenth.
The results are stable across sensitivity analyses. Excluding the 2015–2020 interval raises γ slightly to 1.44 and leaves δ at 1.53. The constant is smaller after 2000 (1.10) than before (1.45), as gains slow at higher life expectancy, while the income slope is larger after 2000 (2.79 versus 1.38). By income group, the constant is largest in low-income countries (1.66) and smallest in high-income countries (0.96); the slope is largest in low-income countries (3.03) and not significant in upper-middle-income countries.

title: Does Income Growth Raise Life Expectancy? Country-by-Country Regressions in Levels and Five-Year Differences
text:
Discussion

Key results
Three findings stand out. First, the levels regressions reproduce, in units, the strong within-country correlations of the previous post: a median of 6.9 more years of life expectancy per doubling of income. Second, those slopes are mostly trend. When the models are written in five-year differences, which move the common trend into the constant, the median slope falls by about 85%, R² falls from 0.81 to 0.08, and the slope is significant in only 12 countries. Third, the constant in the difference model, the expected gain at zero income growth, is positive and large: about 1.3 years every five years on average, roughly nine tenths of the average gain.


How does the change in GDP affect the change in life expectancy?
On average, positively but modestly. Pooled across 106 countries, a country whose income grew 10% faster over five years gained about 0.17 more years of life expectancy. For the typical country, sustained growth of 1.8% per year, close to the sample median, corresponds to about 0.15 years of the roughly 1.5 years gained every five years. The rest of the gain appears in the constant.
This bears directly on the question raised in the previous post: can health improve without income growth? In this model, the constant is that improvement, and it is the larger part of the story. It is consistent with the literature arguing that most of the twentieth-century mortality decline came from the spread of knowledge, technology and public health programs rather than from income as such (Preston, 1975; Caldwell, 1986; Cutler, Deaton and Lleras-Muney, 2006). It is also consistent with the countries in the previous post that gained 20 years of life expectancy while their incomes fell.


Limitations
These are unadjusted associations and should not be read as causal effects. Several limitations apply:

The constant is not policy. γ captures everything that raises life expectancy at a steady pace unrelated to five-year income growth: medical technology, public health programs, education, aid and falling fertility. It identifies room for non-income explanations but does not identify which ones.
Income may act slowly. Differencing over five years captures short- and medium-run associations. If income works through slow channels, such as schooling or health systems built over decades, a five-year model will understate its long-run association, and the levels slope may be closer to the truth than it appears. The two models bracket the answer rather than settle it.
Attenuation. Measurement error in GDP and modeled life expectancy biases slopes toward zero, and differencing amplifies measurement error relative to the signal.
Inference. Levels standard errors are understated because of autocorrelation. Country-specific difference regressions have 12 observations and little power, so the 94 non-significant δ estimates are consistent with small positive effects, not evidence of no effect.
Sample and timing. Requiring 1960 data excludes many countries; the final interval includes the onset of COVID-19; and single extreme intervals, such as China’s famine recovery, can dominate a country’s regression.



Interpretation
The levels regression answers “how much higher is life expectancy when income is higher?” within a country, and its answer, about seven years per doubling, mixes the effect of income with everything else that improved over the same decades. The difference regression asks “when income grows faster than usual, does life expectancy also rise faster than usual?” Its answer is yes, but by a small amount. Read together, the two models suggest that income growth has contributed to the rise in life expectancy since 1960, but that most of the rise would be attributed to the steady improvement captured by the constant.


Generalizability
The estimates describe 106 countries with data from 1960, a group that includes most of Africa, Latin America and Western Europe but few post-1960 states. They describe 1960 to 2020, a period of unusually rapid diffusion of medical technology; a similar regression for an earlier or later period could give a different constant. Pooled estimates are averages across very different countries, and Figure 2 shows that country-specific relationships vary widely.

title: Does Income Growth Raise Life Expectancy? Country-by-Country Regressions in Levels and Five-Year Differences
text:
Conclusion and next steps
A simple OLS regression turns the correlation from the previous post into a size: in levels, about seven years of life expectancy per doubling of income; in five-year differences, about 0.17 years per 10% of faster growth, with most of the gain in the constant. Anchoring the levels model at 1960 income makes its constant interpretable as fitted life expectancy at the starting income; differencing removes that anchor and turns the constant into the gain that occurs without growth. Natural next steps are to add country and year effects to a pooled model, which separates global improvements in each period from country-specific growth; to use longer differences (ten or twenty years) to test whether income acts slowly; and to add measured health inputs, such as vaccination coverage or health spending, to see what the constant contains.
